by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Honey eaten as food, often in place of other sugars

decisions.reason: Updated meta-analysis of RCTs analyses honey on its own, apart from royal jelly and propolis, and reports triglycerides among cardiometabolic outcomes.
Meta-analysis of controlled trials of oral honey intake pooling total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
Meta-analysis of controlled trials of honey consumption pooling cholesterol fractions and triglycerides.

question.population: Children or adults with colds or other upper respiratory infections
question.outcome: Symptoms such as cough, sore throat or congestion

decisions.reason: Pooled studies of honey versus usual care or placebo in people with upper respiratory infections, measuring cough and combined symptom scores.
Reviewed trials of honey versus no treatment or cough medicine in children with acute cough; the one included trial was in upper respiratory infections and measured cough.
Population is children with chronic non-specific cough, not colds or other acute upper respiratory infections, and no studies were found.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Honey eaten as food, often in place of other sugars
question.comparison: Sugar, other sweeteners, or no honey

decisions.reason: Honey is analysed apart from royal jelly and propolis in a meta-analysis of RCTs reporting HbA1c and fasting blood glucose.
Meta-analysis of controlled trials of eating honey, with fasting glucose and other glycemic control results.
Systematic review of trials of eating honey in adults with or without type 2 diabetes, reporting glycemic status.

question.intervention: Honey dressings applied to the skin
question.comparison: Other dressings, silver sulfadiazine or standard care
question.outcome: Healing time, healing rate or infection

decisions.reason: RCTs of honey dressings across wound types, with burns reported as a separate category for healing time and antibacterial effect.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with silver dressings on healing time; the included studies were on burns.
RCTs of honey versus silver sulfadiazine for burns, measuring healing time and infected wounds made sterile.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with other dressings, mostly silver sulfadiazine, for burns, measuring healing at 15 days.

question.comparison: No treatment, placebo or cough medicines
question.outcome: Cough frequency or severity, or sleep

decisions.reason: Meta-analysis of RCTs of honey versus cough medicines in children with acute cough, reporting cough frequency, severity and sleep.
Systematic review of RCTs of honey versus placebo, no treatment or cough medicines in children with acute cough, reporting cough frequency and sleep.
Compares honey with cough medicines in children, but the abstract does not say the cough is short-term or which cough or sleep outcomes were assessed.
Cochrane review of RCTs of honey versus no treatment, placebo or cough medicines in children with acute cough, reporting cough frequency.
Cochrane review of RCTs of honey versus no treatment, placebo or cough medicines in children with acute cough, with pooled cough frequency.
Meta-analysis of randomised trials of honey in children with acute cough, reporting cough severity and frequency and sleep quality.
Cochrane review of honey versus no treatment or dextromethorphan in children with acute cough, reporting cough frequency, severity and sleep.
Cochrane review of RCTs of honey versus no treatment or cough medicines in children with acute cough, with pooled cough frequency.
Reviews honey versus placebo in children, but for chronic non-specific cough rather than short-term cough, and it found no eligible trials.

question.population: People with leg ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers or other wounds

decisions.reason: Mainly a narrative review of how honey works; it compares honey with other topical agents but reports wound area and re-epithelialisation, not clearly healing time or rate.
Systematic review of 22 RCTs of honey dressings on surgical wounds, ulcers and burns that reports shorter healing.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with silver dressings on wounds (all burns), with days to healing as the outcome.
Systematic review of studies of any design on honey for burns, ulcers and other wounds that assesses wound healing.
Cochrane review of RCTs comparing honey with other dressings for acute and chronic wounds, including leg and diabetic foot ulcers; healing is the main outcome.
Cochrane review of trials comparing honey with conventional treatments for acute and chronic wounds, with time to healing as the main outcome.
Systematic review of RCTs comparing topical honey with other treatments for burns and infected postoperative wounds, with healing time as an outcome.
Cochrane review of trials comparing honey with other treatments for acute and chronic wounds, including leg ulcers; healing is the main outcome.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with conventional dressings for diabetic foot ulcers, reporting healing rate and time to healing.
Meta-analysis of honey dressings for chronic wounds that reports healing time and healing rate.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with placebo for obstetric wounds, with wound healing as a main outcome.
Meta-analysis of trials of honey dressings for diabetic foot ulcers that reports wound recovery time and rate.
Meta-analysis comparing honey with povidone iodine dressings for wounds, with healing duration as the outcome.
Meta-analysis of RCTs and quasi-experimental studies of honey dressings for diabetic foot ulcers, reporting healing time and rate.
This is a corrigendum with no abstract, not a review.
Systematic review of RCTs of honey for acute and chronic wounds that reports shorter healing time.
Reviews honey combined with other agents, mostly in lab and mouse studies, for antimicrobial effects; no human healing comparison.
This is a comment on a review with no abstract, not a review.
Systematic review of trials and observational studies comparing topical honey with conventional dressings for diabetic foot ulcers.

question.outcome: Oral mucositis: how often, how severe, or pain

decisions.reason: Meta-analysis of RCTs of honey in head and neck cancer patients having radiotherapy; reports severe mucositis incidence and pain.
Meta-analysis of trials of honey in head and neck cancer patients having radiotherapy; reports mucositis incidence and severity.
Meta-analysis of RCTs of honey in patients having radiotherapy; reports incidence by mucositis grade and pain.
Meta-analysis of honey for children having radio/chemotherapy; reports incidence and severe grades of oral mucositis.
Network meta-analysis of RCTs of honey vs control arms in chemo/radiotherapy patients; reports moderate-severe oral mucositis.
Meta-analysis of RCTs of honey in radiochemotherapy patients; reports mucositis grades and pain scores.
Systematic review of 17 RCTs of honey in head and neck cancer patients having radio/chemoradiotherapy, with oral mucositis outcomes.
Meta-analysis of honey in head and neck cancer patients having radiotherapy; reports mucositis severity and time to onset.
Umbrella review of honey reviews in head and neck cancer patients having radiotherapy; reports oral mucositis incidence and severity.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing honey with blank control in radio/chemotherapy patients; reports oral mucositis incidence.
Guideline systematic review of many agents, with honey judged separately, for preventing oral mucositis in cancer patients having radio/chemotherapy.
Meta-analysis of RCTs of oral honey vs placebo or no treatment in radiotherapy patients; reports mucositis incidence, grade and pain.
Meta-analysis of controlled trials of honey vs control for radiation-induced oral mucositis.
